title: Question 5
stem:
A solid cylinder is lifted out of oil by a wire attached to a motor. Fig. 5.1 shows two different positions X and Y of the cylinder during the lifting process.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The motor is fixed to an overhead beam.
The cylinder has cross-sectional area $0.018\text{ m}^2$, length $1.2\text{ m}$ and weight $560\text{ N}$.
The density of the oil is $940\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.

Throughout the lifting process, the cylinder moves vertically upwards with a constant velocity of $0.020\text{ m s}^{-1}$. The viscous force of the oil acting on the cylinder is negligible.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate the density of the cylinder.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what you actually know about the cylinder - you are given its weight, not its mass, and its size as area and length. How are weight and mass linked, and how do area and length give the space it occupies?
Hint 2: Combine $mass = weight / g$ with $volume = area \times length$ to find $\rho = m/V$, then check units give $\text{kg m}^{-3}$.
parts.proper_answer: Volume $V = 0.018 \times 1.2 = 0.0216\text{ m}^3$, mass $m = 560/9.81 = 57.1\text{ kg}$, $\rho = m/V \approx 2.6 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Sort Out Mass and Volume**
You are given weight in $\text{N}$, but density needs mass in $\text{kg}$. Remember weight is the gravitational force on the mass, so mass is smaller by a factor $g$. Volume is not given directly, but for a uniform cylinder volume is just cross-sectional area times length.

Step 2: **Calculate Density**
First find the numbers: $$m = \frac{W}{g} = \frac{560}{9.81} \approx 57.1\text{ kg}$$ $$V = A L = 0.018 \times 1.2 = 0.0216\text{ m}^3$$ Then density: $$\rho = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{57.1}{0.0216} \approx 2640\text{ kg m}^{-3} \approx 2.6 \times 10^3\text{ kg m}^{-3}$$ to 2 significant figures, matching the data.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: For the cylinder at position X, show that the upthrust due to the oil is $200\text{ N}$.
hints: Hint 1: At position X the cylinder is fully under the oil surface. Think about what upthrust really is - the weight of the oil that would be there if the cylinder was not there. Which density and which volume should you use?
Hint 2: Use $upthrust = density\text{ of oil} \times submerged\text{ volume} \times g$ with the full cylinder volume $1.2 \times 0.018$ and show it rounds to $200\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall What Causes Upthrust**
When an object sits in a fluid, the fluid pressure pushes up more on the bottom than down on the top. The net result equals the weight of fluid displaced. At X the whole cylinder is displaced, so displaced volume equals cylinder volume.

Step 2: **Put Numbers In To Show 200 N**
Displaced volume is: $$V = 1.2 \times 0.018 = 0.0216\text{ m}^3$$ Weight of this oil is: $$U = \rho_{oil} V g = 940 \times 0.0216 \times 9.81$$ $$U \approx 199\text{ N} \approx 200\text{ N}$$ as required. Note you must use oil density $940\text{ kg m}^{-3}$, not cylinder density.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: Calculate, for the moving cylinder at position X,
hints: Hint 1: The cylinder moves up at steady speed, so resultant force is zero. Draw weight down and the two upward supports - tension in the wire and upthrust from the oil - and see how they must balance.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Balance Forces For Steady Motion**
Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so by Newton's first law forces balance. Downward is weight $560\text{ N}$. Upward are tension $T$ plus upthrust $200\text{ N}$. So: $$T + U = W$$ $$T = 560 - 200 = 360\text{ N}$$ The wire only has to provide what upthrust does not.

hints: Hint 1: The cylinder moves up at steady speed, so resultant force is zero. Draw weight down and the two upward supports - tension in the wire and upthrust from the oil - and see how they must balance.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.text: the power output of the motor.
hints: Hint 1: Power is the rate of doing work against the pull of the wire. Think about which force the motor acts with and how fast the point of application moves.
Hint 2: Use $P = Fv$ with $F$ as the tension from (c)(i) and $v = 0.020\text{ m s}^{-1}$ in the direction of the force.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link Power To Tension and Speed**
The motor pulls with force equal to the tension, moving the wire up at $0.020\text{ m s}^{-1}$. For a force parallel to velocity, rate of working is simply force times velocity.

Step 2: **Calculate**
$$P = T v = 360 \times 0.020$$ $$P = 7.2\text{ W}$$ This is the useful output power at position X.

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.part_stem: The cylinder is raised with constant velocity from position X to position Y.
parts.text: State and explain the variation, if any, of the power output of the motor as the cylinder is raised. Numerical values are not required.
hints: Hint 1: As the cylinder rises from X to Y, think about how much of it stays below the oil surface and what that means for the amount of oil displaced.
Hint 2: With weight fixed but upthrust changing, think about how the wire tension must adjust to keep the motion at constant velocity with zero resultant force.
Hint 3: Link the new tension to motor power using $P = Tv$ with $v$ constant to decide if power rises, falls or stays the same.
parts.proper_answer: Upthrust decreases as submerged volume decreases. Tension increases to still balance weight at constant velocity. Power output $P = Tv$ increases as $v$ is constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What Happens To Upthrust**
From X to Y more and more of the cylinder leaves the oil. Submerged volume falls, so weight of displaced oil falls. Hence upthrust decreases, reaching zero when fully out.

Step 2: **What Happens To Tension**
Weight $560\text{ N}$ is unchanged and velocity stays constant, so $T + U = W$ still holds. If $U$ gets smaller, $T$ must get larger to make up the difference.

Step 3: **What Happens To Power**
Motor power is: $$P = T v$$ with $v = 0.020\text{ m s}^{-1}$ constant. Since $T$ increases, $P$ increases. No numbers are needed, just the chain: less displaced volume leads to less upthrust leads to more tension leads to more power.

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.text: The rate of energy output of the motor is less than the rate of increase of gravitational potential energy of the cylinder. Without calculation, explain this difference.

hints: Hint 1: The motor is not the only thing doing work on the cylinder - think about the direction of the upthrust force relative to motion, and where oil moves to as the cylinder vacates space.
parts.proper_answer: Upthrust does work on the cylinder, or equivalently oil loses GPE as it flows down to fill the space left by the cylinder, so part of the cylinder GPE gain comes from the oil, not the motor.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot The Extra Energy Source**
Upthrust acts upward in the same direction as displacement, so it does positive work on the cylinder. Physically, as the cylinder rises, oil flows down to fill the hole it leaves, so the oil itself loses gravitational potential energy. That lost oil energy plus motor work together provide the cylinder GPE gain, so motor power alone is less than $mgv$.
